# Raptor Studio MCP server — guide

Raptor Studio ships a [Model Context Protocol](https://modelcontextprotocol.io)
server, so an AI assistant can build, validate, simulate and explain
reliability block diagrams. It uses the same engine as the desktop app and the
`raptor` command line, and returns full-precision JSON plus Markdown you can
read.

The server is named `raptor-studio`. Its entry points are
`raptor-studio-mcp`, `raptor mcp` and `python -m raptor.mcp`.

> This page is the human guide: install, connect, concepts and recipes.
> The exhaustive per-tool catalogue is generated in
> [`MCP-reference.md`](MCP-reference.md), with every description, parameter,
> return field and example. The tutorial's worked chapter is
> [RAPTOR from an AI Assistant](../new_docs/book.html#ch-mcp).

<a id="at-a-glance"></a>

## At a glance

<!-- BEGIN GENERATED FACTS (tools/gen_mcp_reference.py) -->
- **68 tools** in 7 task groups.  With `--no-render`, which hides the PNG diagram tool, the server exposes **67**.
- **8 resources** (fixed URIs and templates) and **3 prompts**.
- The tutorial book has **24 chapters**; the MCP chapter is book chapter 23 of 24 (source `new_docs/chapters/ch16-mcp.adoc`).
<!-- END GENERATED FACTS -->

- **Start small.** Install the optional `[mcp]` extra, connect one client, and
  call `ping`; the first real model is one `build_model` call away.
- **Everything is a tool.** Models are built and edited through the same
  validation and input rules as the desktop app. A tool call never changes a
  model open in the app: the server works on its own copies in a workspace.
- **Results are data.** Simulations return a `run_id`; reports, tables,
  time series and exports are separate calls, so an assistant can fetch only
  the part it needs.
- **Long jobs do not block.** `start_run` returns a `job_id`; poll
  `run_status`, then read the finished run like any other.
- **Safe by default.** stdio uses no network port. HTTP requires a bearer
  token, checks origins and the Host header, and supports `--read-only`,
  `--allow-read` and `--allow-write`.

<a id="quickstart"></a>

## Quickstart

You need Python 3.12 or newer and an MCP-capable client. Qt's system
libraries are optional: they are needed only for `render_diagram` (PNG); the
SVG renderer and every number work without them.

### 1. Install

```bash
pip install "raptor-studio[mcp]"
```

Or run it without installing anything:

```bash
uvx raptor-studio-mcp --workspace ~/raptor-models
```

From a checkout, use `uv sync --extra mcp` and
`uv run python -m raptor.mcp --workspace ~/raptor-models`.

The desktop installers carry the application only; they do not bundle the
server. Install the `[mcp]` extra (or run `uvx raptor-studio-mcp`) on the
machine that starts the client.

### 2. Connect a client

**Claude Code**

```bash
claude mcp add raptor-studio -- raptor-studio-mcp --workspace ~/raptor-models
```

**Claude Desktop** (`claude_desktop_config.json`), and most other clients
that take a JSON config:

```json
{
  "mcpServers": {
    "raptor-studio": {
      "command": "raptor-studio-mcp",
      "args": ["--workspace", "/home/you/raptor-models"]
    }
  }
}
```

If the command is not on `PATH`, give the full path to the virtual
environment's `raptor-studio-mcp`. From a checkout use
`"command": "uv", "args": ["run", "--directory", "/path/to/repo", "python", "-m", "raptor.mcp"]`.

**OpenCode** (`opencode.json`; OpenCode reloads it when saved):

```json
{
  "$schema": "https://opencode.ai/config.json",
  "mcp": {
    "servers": {
      "raptor-studio": {
        "type": "local",
        "command": ["raptor-studio-mcp", "--workspace", "/home/you/raptor-models"]
      }
    }
  }
}
```

From a checkout, use
`"command": ["uv", "run", "--directory", "/path/to/repo", "python", "-m", "raptor.mcp"]`.
The CLI writes the same entry:
`opencode mcp add raptor-studio -- raptor-studio-mcp --workspace ~/raptor-models`.

To try the tools by hand, the MCP Inspector opens a form for each tool (it
needs Node.js):

```bash
npx @modelcontextprotocol/inspector raptor-studio-mcp --workspace ~/raptor-models
```

### 3. Ping

Call `ping` with an empty argument object:

```json
{}
```

Expected result: `pong`. Then ask `workspace_info` for the root and the
read/write rules:

```json
{}
```

It returns `root`, `allowed_read`, `allowed_write`, `max_models`,
`max_bytes`, `retain_days` and the current block defaults.

### 4. Build, validate, simulate, report

These are tool-call argument objects. Paste one into your client's tool form,
or send it as the `arguments` of `tools/call`. Replace `<model_id>` and
`<run_id>` with the values returned by the previous step.

**Build a one-pump model:**

```json
{
  "name": "Quickstart",
  "spec": {
    "blocks": [
      {
        "name": "Pump",
        "fail_dist": "Exponential",
        "fail_params": [1000],
        "repair_dist": "Exponential",
        "repair_params": [10]
      }
    ],
    "nodes": [
      {"name": "Start", "type": "start"},
      {"name": "End", "type": "end"}
    ],
    "links": [
      {"from": "Start", "to": "Pump"},
      {"from": "Pump", "to": "End"}
    ]
  }
}
```

Expected shape (the ids differ on every run):

```json
{
  "model_id": "m_1a2b3c4d",
  "summary": "1 block(s), 2 node(s)",
  "validation": {"errors": [], "warnings": [], "runnable": true}
}
```

If you already have a model, use `open_model` instead:

```json
{"path": "MotorDemo"}
```

`open_model` accepts a bundled example name like `MotorDemo`, or a path inside
the workspace or an `--allow-read` directory.

**Validate it:**

```json
{"model_id": "<model_id>"}
```

Expected shape:

```json
{"errors": [], "warnings": [], "groups": [], "runnable": true}
```

**Estimate the batch:**

```json
{"model_id": "<model_id>", "num_runs": 100}
```

Expected shape:

```json
{
  "seconds_estimate": 0.27,
  "total_batches": 1,
  "per_run_ms": 2.7,
  "advice": "Fast model — estimated 0.27s for 100 runs; no action needed."
}
```

The real `advice` string may add model-specific caveats (events, workers,
time-varying failure rates); show it as returned rather than trimming it.

**Simulate:**

```json
{"model_id": "<model_id>", "num_runs": 100, "seed": 7}
```

Expected shape (trimmed):

```json
{
  "run_id": "r_5e6f7a8b",
  "model_id": "m_1a2b3c4d",
  "runs": 100,
  "truncated": false,
  "summary": {
    "Availability": {"mean": 0.9903, "sem": 0.0019},
    "Reliability": {"mean": 0.57, "sem": 0.0498}
  },
  "workers": 1,
  "workers_auto": false
}
```

`summary` has min, mean, max, standard deviation and SEM for every metric.
Read `truncated`: a partial batch is noisier than requested.

**Read the report:**

```json
{"run_id": "<run_id>", "section": "final_results", "limit": 20}
```

Expected shape:

```json
{
  "section": "final_results",
  "total": 60,
  "next_offset": 20,
  "lines": [
    "Results from 100 runs of sim time 730.500000:",
    "Availability   0.902604453   0.990341317   1.000000000"
  ]
}
```

For one assessable bundle instead of pages, call
`get_run_results` with the same `run_id`; it returns metric means,
per-replication figures, a capacity summary and the weakest elements.

<a id="concepts"></a>

## Concepts

<a id="workspace"></a>

### Workspace

The workspace is the server's only persistent home. By default it is
`~/.local/share/raptor-studio/mcp` (or under `$XDG_DATA_HOME`); set another
with `--workspace`. It contains:

- `models/` — one directory per open model, with its `.rbds` file, backups and
  undo history;
- `runs/` — completed run artefacts and reports;
- `renders/` — rendered PNG and SVG files;
- `Tables/` — default export folder for spreadsheets, CSV and text.

Every path argument is **relative to the workspace** (or an `--allow-read` /
`--allow-write` directory). Absolute paths and `~` are refused. Use
`workspace_info` when you need the root or the exact rules.

The server is isolated from the desktop app: `open_model` copies a file in,
and edits happen to that copy. Two clients attached to one server share one
workspace, so give each person or project their own server and token.

<a id="ids"></a>

### Model, run and job ids

| Id | Looks like | Comes from | Used by |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `model_id` | `m_1a2b3c4d` | `list_models`, `open_model`, `create_model`, `build_model` | every model tool |
| `run_id` | `r_5e6f7a8b` | `simulate`, `start_run` once complete | reports, tables, time series, exports |
| `job_id` | `job_1a2b3c4d` | `start_run` | `run_status`, `cancel_run` |

Model ids are stable while the workspace keeps the model. Run ids survive a
server restart because their artefacts live in the workspace. Job ids are
in-process only: after a restart the run is still there, but the old job id
is not.

<a id="selectors"></a>

### Selectors

Most edit and analysis tools take a `selector`. A selector is:

- a **name**, for example `"Pump"`;
- a **bare id**, for example `"3"`; or
- a **kind-qualified id**, for example `"Block:3"`, `"Node:2"`,
  `"Event:7"` or `"Hierarchy:900"`.

Names must be unique on their level. A bare id is ambiguous when a block and
a node happen to share it — the file format gives each kind its own id space —
so prefer `Kind:id` in scripts. A selector that matches nothing is an error,
not a silently ignored edit.

Hierarchy ids are used as `level` in `render_diagram` and
`render_diagram_svg`, and as `parent` in edit calls. `parent=0` means the top
level. Read ids and counts from `describe_model(detail="full")`.

<a id="tool-kinds"></a>

### Read-only, writes and destructive tools

Every tool carries an MCP risk hint:

- **read-only** — changes no model. Safe to call repeatedly. Examples:
  `list_models`, `validate_model`, `get_report`, `render_diagram`.
- **writes** — edits a model, writes run results, or exports a file.
  Examples: `add_block`, `connect`, `configure_system`, `simulate`,
  `export_tables`.
- **destructive** — deletes, closes or reverts something. Examples:
  `delete_element`, `close_model`, `delete_file`, `undo_last_edit`,
  `save_model_as` (overwrites an existing export of that name).

Start the server with `--read-only` to refuse tools that create, edit or
delete a model or export a file; opening an existing model, analysis and
simulation stay available. `simulate`, `start_run` and `open_model` still
carry the coarse `writes` hint because they create run or workspace
artefacts — the hint is not the `--read-only` gate. Unknown tool parameters
are rejected rather than ignored, so a misspelt `num_runs` fails loudly
instead of quietly using the default.

<a id="tasks"></a>

## Task guides

<a id="build-edit"></a>

### Build or edit a model

**Start a model** in one of three ways:

- `build_model` — a whole model from a friendly `.rbds` spec, as in the
  [quickstart](#quickstart). It always creates a new model and cannot append.
- `create_model` — a blank model or a ready-made `series`, `parallel` or
  `k_of_n` template.
- `open_model` — copy an existing `.rbds`/`.rbd` or a bundled example such
  as `MotorDemo` into the workspace.

Distribution names, codes and parameter order come from
`list_distributions`. To change what a newly added block starts with, call
`configure_block_defaults` (`action="set"`, `"clear"` or `"list"`); this
changes defaults only, not blocks already in the model.

**Edit it** with the smallest tool that matches the job:

- one element: `add_block`, `add_node`, `add_event`, `add_hierarchy`;
- many at once: `add_elements` (one save);
- links: `connect`, `connect_many`, `delete_link`;
- change fields: `update_element`, `update_elements`;
- restructure: `move_element`, `collapse_selection`, `delete_element`,
  `delete_elements`;
- behaviour: `configure_sparing`, `configure_maintenance`,
  `configure_phases`, `configure_system`, `manage_spare_pools`,
  `manage_resources`, `manage_triggers`, `manage_rates`;
- inspect: `describe_model`, `get_element`, `diff_models`.

`extract_hierarchy` turns one hierarchy into a standalone model (a port
extension) or, with `report_only=true`, lists the boundary hazards first —
shared dependencies, spare/resources pools and streams — and the treatment
each would get. The source model is not changed.

A bulk edit is one save and one undo step:

```json
{
  "model_id": "<model_id>",
  "updates": [
    {"selector": "Pump", "patch": {"name": "Pump A"}},
    {"selector": "Valve", "patch": {"fail_params": [6000]}}
  ]
}
```

Call `get_element` after an edit when you need the full row back, and
`undo_last_edit` / `redo_last_edit` to step through the model's own history.
`build_model` auto-lays-out by default; `auto_layout` re-runs the same
layered layout later.

**Notes and callouts** use `add_annotation`, `list_annotations`,
`update_annotation` and `delete_annotation`. A text, rectangle or ellipse
can anchor `adjacent_to` an element (`location` chooses above/below/left/
right/center); an arrow uses `from_`/`to`. Anchored notes move with
`auto_layout`; ones placed by coordinates stay put. `delete_annotation`
returns the deleted annotation id and its kind.

<a id="validate-simulate"></a>

### Validate and simulate

Always validate before a run. `validate_model` returns:

- `errors` — structural or parameter problems; a run is refused while any
  exist;
- `warnings` — caveats that can make a result misleading;
- `groups` — the same rule collapsed across many elements, which keeps a
  700-error model readable;
- `runnable` — true when the engine will accept the model.

Then estimate, run, and read:

```json
{"model_id": "<model_id>", "num_runs": 200, "importance": "both"}
```

`simulate` validates first, estimates the wall time, and refuses a batch
whose estimate exceeds `timeout_s` unless `confirm_long_run` is true. It
returns `run_id`, `runs`, `requested_runs`, `truncated`, `warnings`,
`caveats` and a `summary` with min/mean/max/stdev/sem per metric.

Use `simulate` for a batch that fits in one tool call, and `start_run` when
it does not:

| | `simulate` | `start_run` |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Returns | finished `run_id` and summary | `job_id` immediately |
| Progress | MCP progress notifications | `run_status` polling |
| Cancel | client cancels the request | `cancel_run` |
| Hierarchy isolation | yes | no |
| Importance override | yes | no |

After a run, `get_run_results` gives the bundle; `get_report` pages one
section; `list_tables` lists the available input and result table keys;
`get_table` returns typed rows for one of them; `get_timeseries` returns
points to plot. `describe_metrics` lists the metric names and units if you
are unsure what a column means.

<a id="analyse"></a>

### Analyse capacity, cost, weak links and importance

Turn on the analyses on the model's system settings, run once, then read the
matching report section:

```json
{
  "model_id": "<model_id>",
  "capacity": true,
  "cost": true,
  "weak_link": true,
  "flow_generated": 100
}
```

| Question | Setting | Read |
| --- | --- | --- |
| How much flow is delivered? | `capacity: true`, `flow_generated`, link `nom_flow`/`max_flow` | `get_report(section="capacity")`, `get_timeseries(series="capacity")` |
| What does it cost? | `cost: true` | `get_report(section="cost")` |
| Which block hurts most? | `weak_link: true` | `get_report(section="weak_link")`, `get_run_results(top=20)` |
| Which block should I improve? | `simulate(importance="both")` or `configure_system` | `get_report(section="importance")` |

Capacity has two different questions. `Availability` means *some* flow got
through; `Capacity_Weighted_Availability` (mean flow / flow generated) is the
delivered fraction, and `Lost_Flow` is what did not arrive. Capacity caps
only bind on links entering a node with `full_flow: false`.

Importance reruns the model with each block unable to fail and with it dead,
then reports Birnbaum, RAW, RRW and Vesely–Fussell with sampling error.
`estimate_runtime` includes the extra batches when `importance` is set, so a
long analysis does not surprise you.

For exact static answers, `analytical_analysis` solves series, parallel,
k-of-n, bridge and hierarchy networks without simulation. It refuses PM,
spares, resources and non-Bernoulli events outright; standby, phases and
dependencies are refused until you say how to treat them (`standby=`,
`phase=`, `dependencies=`). `simulate` is the tool for behaviours the solver
cannot represent.

For failure combinations:

- `single_point_failures` fails each element in turn and reports those that
  take the system down alone;
- `failure_effects` applies one scenario from the all-good state;
- `failure_effects_batch` runs up to 2000 scenarios on one model set-up.

Each scenario starts from all-good: failures do not accumulate across calls.
Name every simultaneous failure in one `fail` list.

<a id="compare-sweep"></a>

### Compare models and sweep a parameter

`compare_models` takes 2–5 model or run ids, runs each (or reuses a run's
cached result), and returns per-metric values, deltas against the first
entry, the best entry per metric, and a Markdown table:

```json
{"models": ["<model_id_a>", "<model_id_b>"], "num_runs": 20}
```

`sweep_parameter` works on copies, so the original model is untouched. The
`field` may be a friendly field name or an indexed form such as
`repair_params[0]`:

```json
{
  "model_id": "<model_id>",
  "selector": "Pump",
  "field": "repair_params[0]",
  "values": [4, 8, 16, 32],
  "num_runs": 20
}
```

Each row carries its `run_id` and `runs` count. If every row is bit-identical,
`all_rows_identical` is true and `warnings` says so — that usually means the
field was never applied, not that the model is insensitive.

<a id="export-render"></a>

### Export and render

- `save_model_as` writes a model into the workspace or an `--allow-write`
  directory. `format` is `rbds` (default) or `rbd`; no extension means the
  format's extension is appended. `.rbd` export validates first.
- `export_tables` writes CSV, fixed-width text, a combined text report, an
  Excel workbook or an ODS workbook. With no `tables`, it exports the default
  set; with no `formats`, it writes one `.xlsx`.
- `export_analytical` solves exactly and writes a spreadsheet with Summary,
  Elements, Curve, Equation and Assumptions sheets. `phase="all"` solves
  every phase.
- `render_diagram` returns a PNG (the only picture-valued tool). `level` is a
  **hierarchy id**, not a depth: `0` is the whole model, `900` is hierarchy
  900. `zoom_to` frames named elements on that level; `highlight` outlines
  them. The result reports `effective_label_px` and `legible`, so a caller can
  tell when to zoom in.
- `render_diagram_svg` draws the same level as SVG text without Qt, which is
  useful on a headless server or when checking layout and connections.

Both renderers accept `theme` (`light`/`dark`) and `routing` (`straight`,
`angled`, `orthogonal`). Renders are content-addressed: an edit changes the
file name, so a cached image can never be stale.

<a id="large-models"></a>

### Large models

A model with hundreds of blocks can spend minutes in set-up before its first
replication, and a batch can run for hours. What helps:

- **Run in the background.** `start_run` returns a `job_id` at once. Poll
  `run_status`; its `phase` is `setting_up` while the model is prepared
  (with `setup`: `stage`, `done`, `total`, `percent`), then `simulating`, so
  a quiet start is not a hang. `cancel_run` stops a job between replications,
  or during set-up; completed replications become a truncated run.
- **Use the cores.** Leave `workers` out and a model of 500+ elements run
  20+ times uses half the machine's cores, at most 8, never fewer than two.
  `simulate` and `start_run` report `workers` and `workers_auto`. Pass
  `workers=1` for the sequential numbers: a multi-core batch is repeatable
  but not bit-identical to a sequential one. This default is the server's
  only; the desktop app and `raptor run` keep theirs.
- **Send big inputs by file.** `build_model` takes `spec_path`, a JSON file
  inside the workspace (or an `--allow-read` directory), instead of an inline
  `spec`. `open_model` already takes a workspace path to a `.rbds` or `.rbd`.
- **Batch the what-ifs.** `failure_effects_batch` runs up to 2000 scenarios
  on one model set-up, each from the all-good state, and reports a bad
  scenario without stopping the rest.
- **Know the HTTP limits.** At most two long jobs (`simulate`,
  `sweep_parameter`, `compare_models`, `start_run`) run at once, and at most
  four `start_run` jobs may be queued or running; a fifth is refused with
  `limit_exceeded`.

<a id="resources-prompts"></a>

## Resources and prompts

Resources are read with `resources/read`; versions with `{...}` take the
arguments shown.

| URI | Type | Contents |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `raptor://examples` | application/json | Bundled example models as JSON. |
| `raptor://models` | application/json | Index of open models (`model_id`, name, counts). |
| `raptor://runs` | application/json | Index of completed runs kept in the workspace (newest first). |
| `raptor://examples/{name}` | text/plain | A bundled example model as `.rbds` text. |
| `raptor://models/{model_id}` | text/plain | The live model as `.rbds` text. |
| `raptor://runs/{run_id}/{section}` | text/plain | A full report section for a completed run. |
| `raptor://docs/{chapter}` | text/plain | A tutorial chapter, or `mcp-guide`, `rbds-format`. |
| `raptor://renders/{name}` | image/png | A rendered diagram PNG by file name. |

Prompts are reusable starting points a client can offer as a template or
slash command:

| Prompt | Arguments | What it does |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `new_availability_study` | `system_description`, `mission_hours` | Start a study from a plain-English description. |
| `explain_model` | `model_id` | Explain an existing model in plain English. |
| `improve_availability` | `model_id`, `target` | Propose and test changes that improve availability. |

The server also has `read_doc` and `search_docs`, so a client that cannot read
resources can still search the shipped documentation. An agent can read this
guide with `read_doc(name="mcp-docs")`, the whole generated catalogue with
`read_doc(name="mcp-reference")`, and the tutorial chapter with
`read_doc(name="mcp-guide")`. The catalogue lists every resource and prompt
with its server description.

<a id="transports"></a>

## Transports, security and options

| Transport | Use | Notes |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `stdio` (default) | The client launches the server as a child process. | Listens on no network port. |
| `http` (Streamable HTTP) | A server shared by several clients, or run in a container. | Default `127.0.0.1:8765/mcp`. |

```bash
raptor-studio-mcp --transport http --port 8765 --token-file ~/.raptor-token
```

### HTTP safety

- **A bearer token is required** (`--token-file` or `--token-env`, at least
  16 characters). Make one with
  `head -c 32 /dev/urandom | base64 > ~/.raptor-token; chmod 600 ~/.raptor-token`.
  The server refuses to start without a token unless
  `--allow-unauthenticated` is given, which is for single-user machines only
  and never applies to a non-loopback `--host`.
- Every request needs `Authorization: Bearer <token>`. A client address that
  sends ten wrong tokens in a minute is locked out for a minute (HTTP 429).
- Browser cross-origin calls are blocked unless `--allow-origin` lists the
  origin. The Host header is checked against DNS rebinding.
- `--tls-cert`/`--tls-key` serve HTTPS. A non-loopback bind refuses plaintext
  HTTP unless `--allow-insecure-http` is given explicitly.
- Request bodies are capped. At most two long jobs run at once, and at most
  four `start_run` jobs may be queued or running.
- `--port 0` picks a free port and prints the URL as the first line of
  output.
- All clients of one server share one workspace, so give each person or
  project their own server and token.

### Options

| Flag | Default | Meaning |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `--workspace DIR` | `~/.local/share/raptor-studio/mcp` | Where models, runs and renders live. |
| `--transport {stdio,http}` | `stdio` | Transport; see above. |
| `--host`, `-p/--port`, `--path` | `127.0.0.1`, `8765`, `/mcp` | HTTP bind address, port and endpoint path. |
| `--token-file FILE`, `--token-env VAR` | none | Bearer token, at least 16 characters (one or the other). Required unless `--allow-unauthenticated`. |
| `--allow-unauthenticated` | off | HTTP: serve loopback with no token (single-user machines only). |
| `--allow-origin ORIGIN` | none | HTTP: allowed browser Origin; repeatable. |
| `--tls-cert FILE`, `--tls-key FILE` | none | HTTP: serve HTTPS. |
| `--allow-insecure-http` | off | HTTP: permit plaintext bearer tokens on a non-loopback bind (not recommended). |
| `--read-only` | off | Refuse every tool that creates, edits or deletes a model or exports a file. Opening, analysing and simulating stay allowed. |
| `--no-render` | off | Do not expose `render_diagram` (PNG). `render_diagram_svg` needs no Qt and stays available. |
| `--allow-write DIR` | none | Extra directory `save_model_as` may write to; repeatable. |
| `--allow-read DIR` | none | Extra directory `open_model` may read from; repeatable. The workspace and examples are always readable. |
| `--retain-days N` | 30 | Days to keep run and render artefacts. Models are kept. |
| `--max-runs N` | 5000 | Hard cap on `num_runs` per call. |
| `--log-level LEVEL` | `INFO` | `DEBUG`, `INFO`, `WARNING`, `ERROR`. |

Nothing outside the workspace is written unless `--allow-write` permits it,
and `open_model` only reads the workspace, bundled examples and `--allow-read`
directories.

<a id="troubleshooting"></a>

## Troubleshooting and FAQ

### `raptor-studio-mcp: command not found`

The command lives in the environment's `bin` folder (`Scripts` on Windows),
not necessarily on `PATH`. Activate the virtual environment, use the full
path, or install with `pipx install "raptor-studio[mcp]"`. From a checkout,
`uv run python -m raptor.mcp` works without installing.

### `No module named mcp` or `No module named raptor`

The server is an optional extra. Install `"raptor-studio[mcp]"`, or from a
checkout run `uv sync --extra mcp`. If you are in a checkout but the client
starts a different Python, give the client the full path to the virtual
environment's `raptor-studio-mcp`.

### The server starts but no tools appear

Check the client's MCP server log, then run the Inspector command in the
[quickstart](#quickstart). A server that exits immediately usually cannot
find the package or the workspace path. `--log-level DEBUG` prints the
startup detail.

### `render_diagram` is missing

The server may have started with `--no-render`, or Qt's system libraries may
be absent. Every other tool still works; use `render_diagram_svg` when you
need a diagram without Qt.

### `path resolves outside the workspace`

File arguments are relative to the workspace. Pass `exports/model.rbds`, not
`/home/you/exports/model.rbds`, or add the directory with `--allow-write`
(for exports) or `--allow-read` (for inputs). Call `workspace_info` to see the
allowed roots.

### Models from the desktop app do not appear

That is deliberate isolation. Use `open_model` with a path inside the
workspace or an `--allow-read` directory; the server copies the file in and
leaves the app's model untouched.

### `simulate` refuses a run as too long

The estimate exceeded `timeout_s` (default 1800 s). Reduce `num_runs`, use
`start_run` for a long batch, raise `timeout_s`, or pass
`confirm_long_run: true` if you really mean it.

### The runtime estimate seems off

`estimate_runtime` times a real pilot and extrapolates. Models whose failure
rate changes over time (growth/decay, phases) can have non-uniform per-run
cost, so the pilot can land off. A multi-core batch is also faster than the
estimate's single-core baseline; the estimate accounts for `workers` with a
contention-aware speed-up, not a perfect one.

### A sweep says all rows are identical

`all_rows_identical` means every row's metrics are bit-identical. That is
usually a field that was never applied — check the selector and field name —
not a model that is insensitive. The `warnings` field says so explicitly.

### Can I run more than one client?

Yes, over HTTP with one token per person or project. All clients share the
server's workspace, so separate servers avoid surprising each other. Long
jobs are limited so one client cannot occupy every core.

<a id="full-reference"></a>

## Full tool reference

[`MCP-reference.md`](MCP-reference.md) is generated from the live server and
lists every tool with:

- its full Markdown description;
- a typed parameter table (name, type, required, schema default, enum);
- the declared return fields;
- an argument example.

It is grouped as Workspace and lifecycle, Build and edit, Analysis,
Simulation and what-if, Diagram and annotations, Results and tables, and Meta
and documentation. Use it when you need the exact parameter or return shape;
use this guide when you need the workflow.

<a id="reporting"></a>

## Reporting problems

Open an issue at <https://github.com/openpowershift/RaptorStudio/issues> with
the client, the tool call and the server's `--log-level DEBUG` output. The
tool list is a tested contract, so a change to it is deliberate and shows in
the diff of the generated reference.
